paragraphs: Week 2 (Sept 11 – 15, Lectures 3 and 4) Teaching and Learning

Limits involving bounded functions: here is a useful theorem for computation that is not in the book --- Suppose that f(x) and g(x) are both defined on an open interval containing a point c (except possible at the point c itself). If f(x) -> 0 as x -> c and g(x) is bounded, then the product function f(x)g(x) -> 0 as x -> c. (See my note named “1001lec03 2022” last year.)
2.4 One-sided limits: intuition and definition (again, delta-epsilon definition will not be tested); Theorem 6 and 7 in the book.

2.5 Continuity: definition of continuity, left continuity, and right continuity; basic types of discontinuity (jump, removable, essential); continuous functions (convention: f is continuous on its domain if it is continuous at every interior point of the domain and is one-sided continuous at every endpoint of the domain); properties (Theorem 8); composition of continuous functions (Theorem 9 and 10); intermediate value theorem (Theorem 11); continuous extension.
2.6 Limits involving infinity; asymptotes: finite limits as x ->  and horizontal asymptotes; infinite limits and vertical asymptotes; oblique asymptotes.
3.1 Derivative at a point: definition and related concepts (slope, tangent lines).

*Here is a common question about continuity in the course over the years, which we will need to make a consistent standard: if a function f(x)=1/x has domain [-1,1] except the origin, then where are its points continuity and discontinuity? Let us use the following standard: it is continuous everywhere in the domain (including the endpoints 1 and -1, at which we may particularly say that f is one-sided continuous), and it has no discontinuity (0 is not in the domain; we only talk about continuity or discontinuity for points in the domain). The textbook did not make clear about this and is even inconsistent sometimes.
